R06-A-01: When a trait is described as highly heritable, many readers hear a claim about destiny: if height or some aspect of temperament is 'mostly genetic', then upbringing can do little to alter it. The inference feels natural, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what heritability measures. Heritability is a statistic about a population, not about a person. It estimates what share of the variation in a trait, across a particular group living in a particular range of environments, can be statistically associated with genetic differences among the members of that group. It says nothing about how much of any one individual's height was produced by genes, a question that is not even coherent, since every centimetre of a person's height required both genes and food. Two consequences follow, and both tend to surprise people. First, heritability depends on the environment in which it is measured. If every child in a group were given exactly the same diet, schooling and care, the remaining differences among them would be largely genetic, and the heritability of almost any trait would rise, not because genes had become more powerful but because the environmental differences had been taken away. Conversely, in a group where some children are well fed and others go hungry, differences in nutrition will account for much of the variation in height, and the measured heritability will fall. Second, a trait can be built almost entirely by genes and still show low heritability. Nearly everyone is born with five fingers on each hand because a developmental programme laid down in the genome builds them; most people who have fewer have lost them through injury. Variation in finger number is therefore mainly environmental, even though the fingers themselves are anything but. The most consequential error concerns differences between groups. Suppose a trait is highly heritable within each of two populations. It is tempting to conclude that the average difference between the populations must also be largely genetic. It need not be. Picture two handfuls of seed taken from the same genetically varied sack, one sown in rich soil and the other in poor soil. Within each plot, differences in height will be largely genetic, since the soil is uniform; between the plots, the difference is due entirely to the soil. High heritability within groups is compatible with a gap between them that has no genetic basis at all. None of this makes heritability useless. Breeders rely on it to predict how quickly a herd will respond to selection, and researchers use it to judge where genetic studies are likely to find something. The fault lies not with the statistic but with the habit of reading it as a measure of fixity. A highly heritable trait may still be changed by changing the environment; short sight is substantially heritable, and spectacles correct it all the same.
R06-A-02: For anyone who thinks of natural selection as a relentless editor of waste, the tail of a peacock is an embarrassment, since it is heavy, conspicuous and awkward in flight, and it makes its bearer easier for predators to spot and harder for him to escape. Darwin treated such ornaments as a problem of their own, and proposed that they spread not because they helped their owners survive but because they helped them mate: females preferred them, and the preference was enough to carry the trait forward. That answer, however, raised a second and more awkward question, namely why females should come to prefer an ornament that makes their mates less likely to survive. One influential reply turns the embarrassment into the explanation. An ornament can work as an honest signal precisely because it is costly. A male in poor condition cannot afford to grow and carry an extravagant tail; only a male with ample reserves, and perhaps with sound inherited qualities, can bear the burden and still thrive. A female who chooses the most lavish display is therefore choosing, without knowing it, the male best able to pay. On this view the cost is not a side effect to be minimised but the very thing that keeps the signal reliable. A cheap signal could be produced by anyone, and a signal that anyone can produce soon carries no information. The idea has been extended well beyond courtship. Some antelope, on spotting a predator, leap high into the air on stiff legs instead of fleeing at once, which looks like a waste of precious seconds. If the leap advertises that the animal is fit enough to outrun any chase, a predator that heeds it saves itself a fruitless pursuit, and the leaper is spared an attack. Here too, the display persuades because it could not be produced by an animal that lacked the quality it advertises. It would be a mistake, though, to treat costliness as the whole story. Theoretical work suggests that what matters is not that a signal is expensive in absolute terms but that it is more expensive for weak individuals than for strong ones; a signal equally costly for all would sort no one. Nor need every ornament be honest. Some preferences may persist simply because females who hold them have sons who inherit the admired trait, a self-reinforcing loop that can carry ornaments well beyond any useful information. The costly signal, in short, explains why many displays can be trusted, not why every display exists.
R06-A-03: A familiar complaint holds that the theory of natural selection is empty at its core. Its slogan, survival of the fittest, seems to define the fittest as those who survive, so that the principle reduces to the statement that survivors survive. A claim that cannot be false, the complaint continues, explains nothing; it merely relabels what happened. The objection is old, and it has a certain surface appeal, but it depends on running together two different things: the record of which organisms in fact left offspring and the properties that made them likely to do so. Consider two moths of the same species, one pale and one dark, resting on bark darkened by soot. The dark moth is fitter in that setting, but not because it happens to have left more offspring. It is fitter because its colouring makes it harder for birds to see, and that is a fact one can establish independently, by measuring how often birds find each kind of moth on each kind of bark. Fitness, properly understood, is a propensity: an expected rate of reproduction given an organism's traits and its surroundings. Like the fragility of a glass, it is a disposition that holds whether or not it is ever displayed. A fragile glass may survive a lifetime on a shelf, and a well-camouflaged moth may die in an unlucky accident; neither fact refutes the disposition. Seen this way, the theory makes claims that could turn out false. It predicts that when the propensities of variants differ, and the differences are heritable, the frequencies of the variants will shift in a direction one can anticipate from an engineering or ecological analysis of the traits. Such predictions are tested constantly, and some fail, which is precisely what a tautology could never do. The distinction also explains why biologists speak of drift: in small populations the lucky can outbreed the fit, and the actual record of reproduction can depart from the expected one. If fitness simply meant survival, drift would be unintelligible, since there would be no gap between expectation and outcome for chance to fill. The critics are not wholly wrong, however. Biologists often measure fitness by counting offspring, because propensities are hard to observe directly, and careless writing can slide from the measurement to the definition. The remedy is not to abandon the concept but to keep the evidence for a disposition distinct from the disposition itself.
R06-A-04: The sterile worker castes of ants, bees and wasps troubled Darwin as much as almost any feature of the living world. A creature that never reproduces cannot pass on whatever traits make it a good worker, so it was hard to see how natural selection could have refined the elaborate behaviour of workers over many generations. Darwin's tentative answer was that selection might act on the family rather than on the individual, much as a breeder who wants a good strain of cattle keeps the relatives of an animal whose worth became clear only after it was slaughtered. The idea was given a precise form only in the twentieth century. A gene that disposes its bearer to help relatives can spread even if the bearer leaves no offspring of its own, provided the help raises the reproduction of relatives who are likely to carry copies of the same gene. What matters is the product of two quantities, the benefit to the relative and the probability that the relative shares the gene, weighed against the cost to the helper. Sterility, on this account, is not an anomaly to be explained away but an extreme point on a continuum of helping, reached when a helper can do more for its genes by raising siblings than by raising young of its own. For a time, a further detail seemed to make the case almost too neat. In ants, bees and wasps, males develop from unfertilised eggs, and a peculiarity of inheritance follows: sisters who share both parents are, on average, more closely related to one another than a mother is to her daughters. If workers are more closely related to their sisters than to their own potential offspring, raising sisters is the better genetic bargain, and sterile castes should arise readily in exactly these insects. The argument was elegant, and it was widely taught. It has not survived well. Termites, whose inheritance has no such peculiarity, have sterile castes too; the queens of many ants and bees mate with several males, which dilutes the relatedness among their daughters; and the great majority of species with this peculiar inheritance are not social at all. The lesson is not that kinship is irrelevant. Workers in social insect colonies typically do raise relatives, and the general principle remains the best account of why they can afford to forgo reproduction. The lesson is rather that relatedness is only one term in the calculation. Ecological conditions that make independent breeding hopeless, such as a scarce nest site that must be defended or food that only a group can gather, raise the benefit of helping and can tip the balance even where relatedness is modest. The special feature of inheritance made a good story, but the more durable explanation lies in the interaction of kinship with circumstance.
R06-A-05: Until late in the twentieth century, many biologists expected that animals as different as a fly and a mouse would be built by largely different sets of genes. Their bodies seemed to have little in common: one has a hard external skeleton, six jointed legs and compound eyes, the other an internal skeleton, four limbs and eyes with a single lens. If form reflects the genes that make it, the reasoning went, such different forms must be made by different genes. What came instead was one of the great surprises of modern biology. A small kit of genes that direct development, deciding where the head goes, where limbs sprout and which segments become which, turned out to be shared, in recognisable versions, across almost the entire animal kingdom. The most striking demonstrations concerned eyes. Eyes had long been thought to have evolved independently many times, so different are the eyes of insects, squid and vertebrates. Yet a gene needed for eye development in mice has a counterpart in flies, and when the mouse version is switched on in the wrong tissue of a developing fly, the fly grows extra eyes, fly eyes, on its legs or wings. The gene does not carry a blueprint of an eye. It acts more like a switch that says, in effect, 'build an eye here', leaving the details of construction to the many other genes that each lineage has in its own repertoire. It is tempting to conclude that the evolution of form is mostly a matter of rewiring old switches rather than inventing new parts, and there is much truth in that. Changes in when and where toolkit genes are turned on can alter the number of segments, the length of a limb or the pattern on a wing without any change in the proteins the genes make. Because a single toolkit gene acts in many tissues, a change to the gene itself would tend to disrupt many structures at once, whereas a change to one of its switches can alter a single structure and leave the rest alone. This helps explain why so much evolutionary change appears to lie in the regulatory regions of the genome. Yet the shared toolkit should not be mistaken for a shared plan. That the same switch triggers eye-building in a fly and a mouse does not mean that their eyes are, in any useful sense, the same organ; the structures downstream of the switch were assembled separately, over hundreds of millions of years, from different materials. Common genes reveal a deep common ancestry of the control system, not a common design for what is controlled. The older view was wrong to assume that different forms require different genes; the newer enthusiasm risks the opposite error, of assuming that similar genes imply similar forms.
R06-A-06: We tend to read the history of life as a long tournament in which the better designed win. On this view a lineage that disappeared must have had some flaw, and the dinosaurs, the textbook losers, are pictured as sluggish and outmoded long before their end. The picture is comfortable because it makes the present inhabitants of the earth look like deserving champions. For the most dramatic episodes in the record it is also misleading. During ordinary stretches of geological time, extinction does seem to track the qualities that adaptation produces: species with narrow diets, small ranges or slow breeding are more likely to vanish when conditions shift, and their places are taken by competitors that cope better. The great mass extinctions, in which a large fraction of species disappeared within a geologically brief interval, seem to follow different rules. Consider the end of the Cretaceous period, when an asteroid struck the earth and the non-avian dinosaurs vanished along with many other groups. What determined survival in the aftermath was not, as far as can be told, excellence at the ways of life that had served well for millions of years. It was the possession of traits that happened to matter in a sudden catastrophe: small body size, a varied diet, the ability to shelter or to wait out a period of darkness and scarcity in a dormant state. Such traits had not been selected for their value in a catastrophe of this kind, which no living lineage had experienced. They were, from the point of view of the crisis, accidents. The consequence is that mass extinctions can redirect the history of life in ways that ordinary selection would not. A group that had been flourishing, and that would probably have continued to flourish under normal conditions, can be swept away, while a group that had been marginal for tens of millions of years inherits an emptied world. The mammals, which had lived in the shadow of the dinosaurs for a very long time, are the familiar example. Their later success says little about whether they were superior to the non-avian dinosaurs in any absolute sense; it says that they passed through a narrow gate that the dinosaurs, for reasons unrelated to their earlier success, did not. This does not mean that mass extinctions are pure lotteries. Survival in them is selective; it simply selects for different things. Nor does it mean that adaptation is unimportant, since the survivors went on to diversify through ordinary selection once the crisis had passed. What it does mean is that the long-run shape of life's history cannot be read as a straightforward measure of design quality. To understand why some groups are here and others are not, we need to know not only how well they fitted their world but also which rare disasters that world happened to contain.
R06-A-07: Debates about the origin of life have long been organised around a chicken-and-egg problem. In every living cell today, the information needed to build proteins is stored in nucleic acids, while the work of copying those nucleic acids is done by proteins. Neither seems able to arise without the other. One family of proposals breaks the circle by giving priority to the molecule that carries information: life began, on this view, when some molecule capable of copying itself appeared, however clumsily, and natural selection among its variants did the rest. A rival family gives priority to chemistry that sustains itself: life began as networks of reactions, perhaps on mineral surfaces near hot springs on the sea floor, that captured energy from their surroundings and kept themselves going long before any of their components stored heritable information. The case for putting the replicator first gained great force from a discovery about RNA, a close chemical relative of DNA. RNA, it turned out, can not only carry information but also catalyse reactions, and the core of the machinery that assembles proteins in every cell is itself made of RNA. A world in which RNA did both jobs, storing instructions and doing chemical work, would dissolve the chicken-and-egg problem, and that protein-building machinery looks very much like a relic of such a world. Replicator theorists add a deeper argument. Without heredity, they say, there is no evolution in any serious sense: a chemical network that merely persists cannot accumulate improvements, because there is nothing to record which variants did better. Metabolism-first theorists reply that the RNA world has a chemistry problem it has never solved. The building blocks of RNA are intricate molecules, hard to make without the help of enzymes and prone to fall apart in water; assembling them into long chains that can copy themselves requires a degree of order that seems unlikely to arise unaided. Self-sustaining reaction networks, by contrast, need only simple ingredients and a source of energy. These theorists also argue that heredity need not wait for a dedicated molecule. A network in which certain reactions reinforce one another could persist in several alternative states, and if fragments that break away from a network tend to restart the same state, something like inheritance exists before any gene. It is worth noticing that the two camps are often answering different questions. Replicator theorists ask what made open-ended evolution possible, and their answer, a molecule that copies information with modest accuracy, is hard to dispute as an account of that threshold. Metabolism theorists ask where the materials and energy for any such molecule came from, and their answer, a geochemical setting that drives reactions without the help of life, is equally hard to dispute as an account of the prior stage. Presented as rivals, each side scores easy points against the other's weakest claim: that replicators could assemble themselves in a chemical vacuum, or that self-maintaining networks could evolve indefinitely without anything like genes. The more promising view, then, treats the problem as one of sequence rather than of priority in the abstract. A chemistry able to sustain itself may have been the setting in which the first replicators formed and on which they depended, and the replicators may in turn have captured and refined the network that fed them. This does not settle the matter, since the details of each stage remain obscure and may never be recovered from a planet whose earliest rocks have been largely destroyed. But it changes what counts as progress. The question is no longer which came first, as though one of them had to be the true beginning, but how a world of self-maintaining chemistry could have given rise to one in which information was inherited.
R06-A-08: Suppose the history of life could be rewound to some early point and allowed to run again. Would anything like the present living world appear a second time? One school answers no. Evolution, on this view, is a chain of contingencies, each step dependent on the particular steps before it and on unrepeatable accidents of climate, geology and mutation. Alter any early link, and the chain would run off in another direction entirely; the existence of vertebrates, of flowering plants or of our own species would be no more to be expected than a particular sequence of cards in a shuffled deck. On this view the tree of life is a record of accidents, intelligible after the fact but not predictable before it, and any search for a direction in it reads our own presence back into a history that never had us in mind. The rival school points to the remarkable frequency with which evolution arrives at the same solution independently. Camera-like eyes have arisen separately in vertebrates and in octopuses; streamlined bodies have evolved in fish, in extinct marine reptiles and in dolphins; flight has been achieved by insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats. If the same designs keep recurring, the argument runs, the outcome of a second run would be broadly familiar. Each school has a strong case, and each tends to treat the other's evidence as anecdote. Convergence enthusiasts can list hundreds of cases, but the list is assembled after the fact from the solutions that did recur, and it says nothing about the far larger number of forms that appeared once and never again. Contingency enthusiasts can point to those unrepeated forms, but they often treat the mere fact that a lineage had a particular history as proof that its outcome depended on that history, which does not follow: a ball may take a unique path down a hillside and still come to rest in the only hollow at the bottom. Much of the disagreement, I want to suggest, dissolves once we notice that the two schools are describing life at different levels of detail. At the level of broad functional solutions, a second run would very probably produce organisms that see, swim, fly and filter food, because the physical problems of moving through water or air, or of forming an image from light, admit only a few good solutions. At the level of particular lineages, the replay would almost certainly differ: there is no reason to expect that the flying creatures would be birds, or that the swimmers would have backbones. Convergence is a claim about the space of workable designs; contingency is a claim about which occupants of that space history happens to supply. The two are compatible, and both are probably true. This reconciliation has a cost, and it is worth stating plainly. If the question that matters is whether a replay would produce something like us, a self-aware animal that makes tools and uses language, then neither school's best evidence is decisive. Intelligence of our kind has arisen, so far as we know, only once, and a single case cannot reveal whether it was a likely destination or a fluke. The recurrence of eyes and wings tells us that some problems have few solutions; it does not tell us that every capacity we value is among those solutions. On the questions that most excite the public, the honest answer is that the evidence does not yet discriminate between the two views.
